 JPMorgan says Bitcoin price drop widens gap to $86,000 production cost
 J.P. Morgan logo (Wikimedia Commons, public domain)
 With Bitcoin below $60,000, the market price now sits more than $26,000 under the bank's estimated cost to mine a coin
 by 
 Vivian Nguyen 
 Fri 20 Nov 2026 · 13:25 EST 
 · 
 3 min read 
 In Bitcoin

 Mining a Bitcoin costs about $86,000, according to JPMorgan . The market currently values it far lower.
 The bank’s estimate of Bitcoin’s production cost now sits more than $26,000 above the market price. That gap could push higher-cost miners to sell more of the coins they’ve been holding in reserve.
 The numbers behind the squeeze
 JPMorgan analysts led by Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou published the report on Wednesday. Their central estimate puts Bitcoin’s production cost at $86,000.
 When the note came out, Bitcoin was trading near $65,000. That left a shortfall of about $21,000 between what the asset fetched and what it costs, on average, to produce.
 Two days later, things got worse. On Friday, Bitcoin slipped below $60,000 for the first time since July, stretching the gap past $26,000.
 For Bitcoin miners, the electricity bills and hardware costs don’t pause when prices fall. The coins they mine are worth less, but the inputs cost the same.
 Why prices fell in the first place
 JPMorgan didn’t pin the decline on mining economics alone. The analysts pointed to several broader forces weighing on the market.

 First, crypto exchange-traded funds saw significant outflows. According to the report, retail investors have been rotating out of crypto ETFs and into stock ETFs.
 Second, technology stocks have been deteriorating. Bitcoin has often traded in sympathy with risk assets, so weakness in tech tends to spill over.

 Third, expectations around Federal Reserve rate cuts have shifted. When the market prices in fewer or later cuts, speculative assets tend to lose some of their appeal.
 The miner math
 JPMorgan suggested that many unprofitable miners may be forced to sell their Bitcoin reserves. Some would sell to cover operating costs. Others might sell to fund a pivot into other businesses, such as artificial intelligence.
 JPMorgan’s production cost figure has also moved around this year. Earlier estimates in 2026 ranged from $77,000 to $85,000 before landing at the current $86,000.
 That upward drift means the bar for profitability has been rising even as the price has been falling. Miners are getting squeezed from both directions.
 The soft floor theory
 There’s a reason analysts watch production cost so closely. Historically, it has tended to act as a soft floor for Bitcoin’s price.
 The logic runs like this. When price falls well below cost, the least efficient miners shut off their machines. Fewer machines means less total computing power securing the network, a measure called hashrate.
 Bitcoin then adjusts its mining difficulty to match. When fewer miners compete, the puzzle gets easier, and the remaining miners earn coins more cheaply.
 The JPMorgan analysts said the gap between price and production cost could narrow if higher-cost operations exit. In that scenario, hashrate and difficulty would adjust downward, lowering the average cost to mine.
 Note the word “soft.” A soft floor is not a guarantee. Price can trade below production cost for extended periods, and it often does during bear phases.
 What this means for investors and miners
 For traders, the immediate concern is supply. If struggling miners dump reserves to stay afloat or fund AI pivots, that selling lands on a market already dealing with ETF outflows and nervous macro conditions.
 For mining companies, the divide between efficient and inefficient operators is about to get sharper. Firms with cheap power and newer hardware can ride out a stretch below the average cost. Those near the top of the cost curve face harder choices: sell coins, cut operations, or change business models entirely.
 The macro backdrop still matters, too. JPMorgan tied part of the selloff to tech weakness, ETF rotation, and shifting Fed expectations.
 For now, the gap stands at more than $26,000 and the miners are the ones holding the bill.
